clue.text: Carry on Sir deplorably impounded by pain in the arse

indicators.note: impounded means shut in a pound, so the reordered letters are shut inside the pest word

parts.note: a pest is an annoying person, a pain in the arse

indicators.note: deplorably means very badly, so the letters of Sir are badly placed and must be reordered

parts.note: the word whose letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A knight behaves badly and is locked up by an irritating official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carry on' looks like a link or a film title, but it is the definition; 'deplorably' scrambles the knight's title into RSI, which is 'impounded by' the pest.
explanation.definitionFit: To persist is to continue doing something steadily despite opposition, which is to carry on.

clue.text: All together: let's start to penetrate stupid bone head of Cameron!

indicators.note: to penetrate is to get inside, so the opening letter goes into the reordered bone letters
stupid means senseless, so the letters of bone are put into a senseless new order

parts.note: the word whose letters are rearranged

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose opening letter is taken

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: David Cameron, the former Prime Minister; only his initial is used

explanation.surface: A satirical call to pierce the thick skull of David Cameron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupid' rearranges BONE into ENBO; 'start' gives L, which goes inside to make ENBLO, and 'head of' adds C.
explanation.definitionFit: En bloc is a French borrowing meaning as one group, all together, as when a committee resigns en bloc.

clue.text: Nigel's last gasp UKIP resort "Right for Independence", which is ignitable

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters are put into a new order
Nigel's last is the last letter of his name, the final letter of Nigel

parts.note: Nigel Farage, UKIP's leader; the 's is possessive and only his name is used

indicators.note: one letter put in for another takes its place, so the right letter replaces the independence letter

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange
the UK Independence Party, taken here as letters
I is the abbreviation for Independence, as in the I of UKIP

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage's party, gasping its last, falls back on a right-wing slogan about independence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right for Independence' swaps the I in GASP UKIP for R; with L, the last letter of Nigel, 'resort' rearranges the nine letters. UKIP was the UK Independence Party, led by Nigel Farage.
explanation.definitionFit: A spark plug produces the spark that ignites fuel in an engine; the definition plays on the plug being able to ignite.

clue.text: Bastard whose name can't be remembered

definitions.note: The second definition is a relative clause describing a person rather than a noun; read it as 'person whose name can't be remembered'.
definitions.meaning: a euphemism for someone unpleasant, used in place of the ruder word
the same stock phrase is the placeholder for a person whose name escapes the speaker

explanation.surface: An illegitimate child nobody can put a name to.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one description of a nameless foundling. The euphemism is the link: the polite so-and-so replaces 'bastard', and the same words fill in for a forgotten name.
explanation.definitionFit: So-and-so is both a mild stand-in for an insult like bastard and a placeholder for someone whose name you cannot recall.

clue.text: Balls provided with drug stimulant to achieve an erection?

parts.note: Ed Balls, Labour's shadow chancellor in 2015
'provided' and 'if' both set a condition
ice is street slang for crystal methamphetamine, a stimulant

explanation.surface: Testicles dosed with a pill to get a man going: the Viagra joke Private Eye cannot resist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' at the start of a sentence hides its capital: it is Ed Balls, the politician. The question mark lets 'an erection' mean a building instead of what the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: An erection in its formal sense is anything built or erected, and an edifice is a large building.

clue.text: Cover up a Spice Girl's spot?

indicators.note: In a down entry, 'up' sends letters climbing from the bottom, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: Emma Bunton, 'Baby Spice' of the 1990s pop group
a cover is a LID, reversed

explanation.surface: Concealer on a pop star's pimple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover up' and 'spot' both pull toward make-up over a blemish. The spot is the tight corner you are in, and the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a spot means being in an awkward situation, and a dilemma is a situation with no good way out.

clue.text: see 9dn.
Like Campbell's lot, say, causing conflict, holding up boozer

indicators.note: the conflict word holds the reversed pub inside it

parts.note: to clash is to come into conflict, so a clash is what causes conflict here

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub, and an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A Scottish family causing a feud while propping up the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns INN into NNI, which CLASH is 'holding'. The Campbells are a Scottish clan, famous for the Glencoe massacre, so their lot behaves clannishly.
explanation.definitionFit: Clannish means loyal to one's own close group and wary of outsiders, as Scottish clans such as the Campbells were.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) Concur IMF row loomed over organisation whose chief contribution to global improvement is hot air?

definitions.text: organisation whose chief contribution to global improvement is hot air?

indicators.note: Something knocked over is upset, so the letters before it tumble into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, all 18 letters

explanation.surface: An International Monetary Fund quarrel hanging over a body that mostly talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row loomed over' reads as a news report on the IMF; only 'over' is instruction, the rest is letters. The definition is the Eye's sneer at the annual Davos gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: The World Economic Forum is the organisation behind the Davos summit, and calling its contribution hot air mocks it as a talking shop.

clue.text: 'Bluster' party introduced by supporter (very American)

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
the usual abbreviation for very
the usual abbreviation for American
a do is an informal party

explanation.surface: A loud-mouthed party brought forward by one of its backers, very much in the American style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' next to 'party' suggests a political backer; here it is the undergarment. The brackets hold two abbreviations, V and A, dropped between the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is a show of boldness meant to impress, much the same thing as bluster.

clue.text: Cowboy's dangly thing produced a trial

indicators.note: Something produced has been made up out of materials, so the letters of the phrase are made into a new word

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A cowboy's private parts turned out to be evidence in a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dangly thing' pushes the Eye's usual smut, but the cowboy's dangly thing hangs from his saddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A lariat is a cowboy's lasso, the looped rope he carries hanging at his side.

clue.text: (& 14ac.) Labour free to come undone?

parts.note: labour is toil, a four-letter word for a job
to set free is to release, a five-letter word for unfastened or untied

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the Labour Party, left to itself, would fall apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L turns 'Labour' into the party, but it is plain toil. The question mark admits that free labour coming undone is the surface's political jab.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that works loose gradually comes free of its fixing, which is coming undone.

clue.text: see 26ac.
see 12ac.
Ex-president's after a lead from Monica to "jump"

indicators.note: Coming after something puts it later in the line, so the president's name follows the other pieces
A lead is what goes in front, so the first letter of the name is taken

parts.note: the word as written
the first letter of Monica
George Bush, either of the two former US presidents

explanation.surface: A former president going after a lead from Monica Lewinsky for a quick leap into bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Monica Lewinsky belongs to Clinton, which makes a solver reach for him; the ex-president wanted is Bush. The quoted 'jump' is the attack sense, not the leap.

clue.text: Genesis augmented by Thatcher for a spot

indicators.note: Something augmented has extra added onto it, so the second piece is tacked on the end of the first

parts.note: a genesis is a birth or beginning
Mark Thatcher, Margaret Thatcher's son

explanation.surface: The Book of Genesis padded out by Mrs Thatcher to fill a slot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' sounds like Margaret; the name wanted is her son, Mark. Genesis is the beginning, not the book or the band.
explanation.definitionFit: A birthmark is a coloured patch on the skin present from birth, a kind of spot.

clue.text: Green fiasco — storing cool energy for Telford, maybe

indicators.note: storing means keeping inside, so the jumbled letters hold the cool-and-energy letters
a fiasco is a complete mess, so the letters of green are messed into a new order

parts.note: the word whose letters are rearranged
in means fashionable, cool
E is the physics abbreviation for energy

explanation.surface: A green energy project goes wrong while trying to store power.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Telford was a celebrated Scottish civil engineer who built bridges, roads and canals; 'fiasco' jumbles GREEN into ENGER, which stores INE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford was a great civil engineer, so he is an example, which the 'maybe' flags.

clue.text: Board member makes £1000 by day's end

indicators.note: One thing by another stands next to it, so the thousand sits right beside the second piece

parts.note: K is short for a thousand, as in a £40K salary
night is what the day ends in

explanation.surface: A company director taking home a grand a day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board member' suggests a company director drawing fees; the board is a chessboard. 'Day's end' is a whole word, not a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight is one of the pieces on a chessboard, so a board member in the game sense.

clue.text: Parliament takes nothing from volatile Lady T, now

indicators.note: volatile means unstable and changeable, so the letters are unsettled into a new order
takes, with from, says a letter is subtracted from the pool before it is rearranged
from names the pool, Lady T now, that the nothing letter is taken out of

parts.note: the letters of Lady T and now, rearranged once a letter is taken out
O is the round figure nought, nothing

explanation.surface: A legislature gains nothing from Lady Thatcher's present unpredictable mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes nothing from' asks you to take O out of LADY T NOW, and 'volatile' rearranges the rest. The Tynwald is the parliament of the Isle of Man; Lady T is Margaret Thatcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Tynwald is the ancient legislature of the Isle of Man, one of the oldest continuous parliaments.

clue.text: (& 25ac.) Partner screws for health

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Screws' is Private Eye's crude verb in the surface and a twisting instruction in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Your other half is an informal British phrase for your spouse or partner.

clue.text: Vatican: "Break Eye's resolution!"

the magazine's name with the possessive 's dropped, leaving its three letters for the mix

explanation.definitionFit: The Holy See is the Pope's jurisdiction as a sovereign entity, run from the Vatican, so the two names stand for each other.

clue.text: Become bloody thick male, and get in the habit

he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A stupid bloke turning into an idiot and settling into a routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody thick male' reads as a string of insults for a bloke. The habit is a monk's or nun's robe.
explanation.definitionFit: To clothe someone is to dress them, and getting into a habit is putting on a monk's or nun's robe.

clue.text: Description of Necker Island? It's quite uncultivated

definitions.meaning: Necker Island is owned by Richard Branson, founder of the Virgin group, so its ground belongs to his brand
land that has never been ploughed or farmed

explanation.walkthrough: The capital V is the hidden joke: the first reading wants Branson's company, the second the ordinary adjective. The question mark marks the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgin soil means ground that has never been cultivated, and Necker, being Branson's, is soil owned by Virgin.

clue.text: Hague's second houses speculation

parts.note: haGUE'S Second

clue.text: see 20ac.

clue.text: Anticipating 'New' Tony's entrance, outlandish Saint Mo!

the first letter of Tony
the word as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'New' and Tony point to New Labour and Tony Blair, and Mo to Mo Mowlam of his cabinet. Here Mo is just short for moment.

clue.text: Like making a retreat in offensive holy war

indicators.note: in places the reversed word inside the offensive word

explanation.definitionFit: The Crusades were medieval Christian military campaigns to the Holy Land, so a crusade is a holy war.

clue.text: Bloody hell, the French! They're a nuisance vote-seeking politicians have to deal with

definitions.text: They're a nuisance vote-seeking politicians have to deal with

parts.note: heck is the mild stand-in for hell
les is French for 'the' before a plural noun

explanation.surface: A British politician swearing at the French, pictured as a nuisance to deal with.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark splits the clue: the swearing is wordplay, and everything after it is the definition, pointing at an election campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: Heckles are interrupting shouts from an audience, the nuisance every candidate on the stump faces.
